description: We are a group of NCSSM Students with a diverse set of interests spanning music theory, computer science, mathematics, and earth science.
summary:
GeoSonix is an immersive auditory and spatial web platform that translates NASA Earth science data into a fully interactive soundscape. We developed a multi-sensory virtual globe where users "walk" the planet using keyboards, touch, or voice commands, experiencing real-time satellite data such as precipitation, vegetation, and surface heat through distinct musical instruments, directional audio cues, and haptic feedback.

Traditional Earth science visualization is overwhelmingly visual, leaving out blind and visually impaired users. GeoSonix bridges this gap by transforming complex satellite metrics into intuitive sounds and spoken orientations, allowing for explanations via a hands-free SI assistant and easy-to-use keyboard hotkeys. These features are explained via an introduction video and screen reader settings.

This project democratizes planetary awareness. By making NASA's environmental data accessible through hearing and touch rather than simply through visuals, GeoSonix ensures that critical climate and geographic information is truly inclusive, fostering a deeper connection to our changing planet for everyone.
details:
What GeoSonix Does & How It Works

GeoSonix is a web platform that lets you hear the world. GeoSonix turns the planet into an acoustic canvas. Of only looking at maps GeoSonix lets you walk the earth by ear:

Spatial Audio Navigation: A soft pulse starts from home (Null Island, 0°N 0°E). Moves between your ears to show the direction of home. The pulse fades as you travel farther.

The Earth Orchestra: Real NASA satellite data is turned into music. Rain is played by a violin (GPM IMERG) land heat by a cello (MODIS) plants by a flute (MODIS) ocean heat by a clarinet (GHRSST) and wind by a sound (MERRA‑2). Intensity shows in volume and a shiver or tremble effect when levels are extreme.

Movement & Time Travel: Move with the keyboard (arrow keys or WASD) a touch joystick or voice commands. World‑wrapping lets you go east and appear in the west. You can also go up to 30 days in daily or weekly steps or use "Then & now" (T) to hear what the same calendar day sounded like 20 years ago.

The GeoAssistant (G): A hands‑free guide powered by Claude Haiku. GeoAssistant teaches you the controls answers questions in spoken sentences (20–35 words) and runs commands such as switching layers changing dates or muting.

Benefits & Intended Impact

True Accessibility: Traditional GIS and Earth science tools are mostly visual which excludes blind or visually impaired users. GeoSonix offers screen‑reader compatibility, keyboard navigation, haptic vibration feedback on touch devices and a dedicated screen‑reader mode so audio announcements do not clash with the natural voice‑over.

Visceral Planetary Awareness: By turning numbers such as surface temperature or precipitation into music and spatial cues GeoSonix makes complex environmental data feel intuitive and emotionally resonant.

Democratizing Science: GeoSonix lowers the barrier to learning climate metrics making NASA’s open‑source Earth data engaging for students, researchers and everyday explorers of all abilities.

Tools, Coding Languages and Software Used

Data Sources & APIs: NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services) GPM IMERG (precipitation) MODIS (land surface temperature & vegetation index) GHRSST (sea surface temperature). Merra‑2 (wind speed).

AI & Voice Services: Claude Haiku 5.5 (via api/guide.js) powers the GeoAssistant guide. OpenAI Text‑to‑Speech, with browser speech synthesis fallbacks and audio caching provides vocal feedback.

Web Architecture: GeoSonix is a web app made for desktop, tablet and mobile. It uses web audio APIs to render spatial sound a 3D rotating globe view and a background‑loading system for instant layer switching.

How the Project is Creative

Translating Data into Music: than plotting points on a chart GeoSonix treats planetary systems as an orchestra. Hearing a spike in the cello (land heat) or violin (rain) gives a new artistic way to see weather and climate.

Spatial Homing via Ear: Using ear‑panning for the Null Island pulse lets users navigate blindfolded or purely through sound turning orientation into a sensory game.

Acoustic Time Travel: The "Then & now" feature lets users literally listen to the climate history of a coordinate across a 20‑year span turning data comparison into a flashback.

Key Factors Considered by the Team

Cognitive & Sensory Load: Audio can quickly become overwhelming so the team added a " waves box" for visual clarity made music dip automatically when someone speaks and kept assistant responses short (20–35 words) for clear voice pacing.

Performance & Responsiveness: To keep lag away while exploring data all layers load in the background at startup allowing instant switching, between environmental metrics. Common text‑to‑speech phrases are cached for near‑zero latency.

Universal Usability: The team paid attention to multi‑platform compatibility (desktop keyboard shortcuts, touch joystick controls and responsive mobile design) and strong accessibility fallbacks (browser TTS backup, screen‑reader mode and reduced‑motion support).
